headline: Hochul Discovers Data Centers Are Good, Actually
subheadline: New York's governor positions herself as the Democrat willing to admit the tech industry funds elections.
source_headline: Kathy Hochul's business-friendly data center plan
body_html:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has discovered something remarkable: data centers can be good for business. In a move that can only be described as a Democratic governor's desperate bid to appear reasonable to the venture capital class, Hochul is positioning herself as the leader of an entirely fictional Democratic search for a data center position that "isn't explicitly anti-business." The implication, naturally, is that most Democratic governors are explicitly anti-business—a narrative so useful to tech lobbyists that one wonders if they workshopped it themselves before handing it to Axios.

What makes this positioning delicious is the fundamental dishonesty baked into its premise. Hochul claims her data center platform "isn't being designed with politics in mind." This is, of course, purely political. The statement is a direct appeal to tech investors and operators who have been forced to pretend that their expansion plans are driven by anything other than real estate arbitrage, tax incentives, and regulatory capture. Data centers don't care about partisan philosophy; they care about cheap power, lax environmental oversight, and politicians willing to call it "business-friendly" instead of "captured." Hochul is simply offering the translation service.

The broader context reveals a party in freefall trying to recover donor relationships. As candidates across the country scramble—the word "scramble" doing heavy lifting here—Democratic politicians are now openly competing for the privilege of being the one willing to roll over for tech infrastructure. This isn't new behavior, but the explicit framing of it as a leadership position is a new low. Hochul isn't leading; she's surrendering, and calling it strategy. The fact that this qualifies as newsworthy reveals how far the baseline has shifted.

Consider what "business-friendly" actually means in this context: minimal environmental review, fast-track permitting, subsidized electricity, and politicians who will defend it on cable news without flinching. Hochul's platform is a masterclass in rhetorical laundering. By claiming her approach isn't political, she's making it entirely political—a calculated move to separate herself from the Democratic base that actually objects to data centers for reasons like energy consumption, land use, and climate impact. Those concerns aren't anti-business; they're just inconvenient to the industry.

The track record of similar deals suggests Hochul should be careful what she wishes for. States that have bent over backward to attract data center capacity have typically seen the benefit accrue to out-of-state operators while bearing the infrastructure and environmental costs locally. Tax incentives evaporate, promised jobs materialize at a fraction of projections, and the energy grid strains under the load. But none of that matters as long as Hochul gets credit for being "reasonable" in the eyes of people who fund her next campaign.

What this moment really represents is the complete rewiring of Democratic electoral strategy around tech industry appeasement. Data centers have become the Trojan horse through which venture capitalists and infrastructure operators funnel money into Democratic coffers while maintaining plausible deniability about regulatory capture. Hochul isn't inventing a new position; she's just being honest about which side of the industry line her party has landed on.

Nothing says leadership like competing with other Democrats to prove you're the least bothered by AI-powered environmental destruction.
glossary_definition: A political term meaning 'willing to subordinate environmental and community concerns to private sector expansion plans without calling it what it is.'
